title: Hydrodynamics of perceptual matter: from neural representations to collective motion
abstract: How do neural representations of neighbors become collective material behavior? Harmonic Theory (HT) reduces bearing representations to signed perceptual channels traceable to sensory acuity, decision dynamics, and interaction distance. Here we derive a nonlocal kinetic and hydrodynamic theory from the HT particle law without introducing heading alignment. The resulting fields retain HT's order-resolved perceptual spectrum and keep the neural and sensory origin of each coefficient visible. The theory predicts a torque-driven density instability: HT's direct-approach channel turns agents toward density excesses, while self-propulsion carries them inward. For isotropic spatial interactions and positive rotational diffusion, perceptual channel $n$ generically first affects conserved density at spatial order $k^{2n}$, and the full radial transforms select finite pattern wavelengths. Two populations can share the same long-wave instability threshold yet select different initial pattern spacings because their higher perceptual channels differ. Beyond onset, the one-particle continuum sustains a bidirectional nematic column; a prescribed, symmetry-allowed two-stream response amplifies a directional imbalance into sustained polar flow. In a distinct pure-repulsion regime, one-particle calculations show polar transport and translating transverse bands, with late pattern selection sensitive to numerical transport. The framework connects neural and sensory mechanisms to continuum coefficients, instabilities, and alignment-free collective motion.
summary: This paper develops a comprehensive hydrodynamic theory for active matter, treating collective motion as 'perceptual matter' derived from neural models. It successfully bridges the gap between individual agent perception and macroscopic continuum behavior by deriving stability criteria and transport equations. The work is significant for showing how specific sensory and decision mechanisms dictate collective instabilities and flow patterns.
main_problem: To derive a nonlocal kinetic and hydrodynamic theory connecting neural representations (from Harmonic Theory) to macroscopic collective material behavior without assuming explicit heading alignment.
main_result: The theory predicts a torque-driven density instability and successfully links macroscopic continuum coefficients to microscopic sensory and decision-making factors.
method: The authors derive the continuum theory by applying closure approximations and moment expansions to the particle-level stochastic differential equation derived from the Harmonic Theory particle law.
model_or_system: The system models 'perceptual matter'—the collective motion of agents whose turning behavior is governed by how their neural representations of neighbors' bearings and distances influence their movement.
key_observables: Density ($ho$), polarization ($f_1$), and the eigenvalues ($\lambda$) derived from linear stability analysis.
important_parameters: Perceptual channels ($q_n$), sensory acuity ($c_n(\sigma)$), decision dynamics ($M_n(W)$), and interaction distance ($J(r)$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumptions include the molecular chaos closure approximation and the rapid relaxation of the decision bump relative to sensory changes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the scale-by-scale route from perception to material dynamics, connecting perceptual harmonic coefficients to continuum transport equations.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from the microscopic particle law (SDE) to a kinetic field description, then uses moment expansion and Fourier transforms to derive the macroscopic, closed hydrodynamic equations, culminating in a linear stability analysis.
why_interesting: While focused on active matter, the rigorous derivation of macroscopic equations from underlying microscopic rules, coupled with stability analysis, shares methodological parallels with non-equilibrium statistical mechanics used in quantum many-body systems.
